claim: Transmission of SARS-CoV-2 from humans to other species threatens wildlife conservation and may create novel sources of viral diversity for future zoonotic transmission.
source: Transmission of SARS-CoV-2 from humans to other species threatens wildlife conservation and may create novel sources of viral diversity for future zoonotic transmission.
evidence: This is a general statement about the implications of SARS-CoV-2 transmission, drawing on established scientific understanding of zoonotic disease dynamics.

claim: Variation in ACE2 can be used by machine learning models to accurately predict animal susceptibility to sarbecoviruses with an accuracy of 80.2% (binomial confidence interval [CI]: 70.8–87.6%).
source: Using a newly compiled database of 96 species, we show that, while variation in ACE2 can be used by machine learning models to accurately predict animal susceptibility to sarbecoviruses (accuracy = 80.2%, binomial confidence interval [CI]: 70.8–87.6%), the sites informing predictions have no known involvement in virus binding and instead recapitulate host phylogeny.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from machine learning models trained on a database of 96 species.

claim: The sites in ACE2 informing predictions have no known involvement in virus binding and instead recapitulate host phylogeny.
source: Using a newly compiled database of 96 species, we show that, while variation in ACE2 can be used by machine learning models to accurately predict animal susceptibility to sarbecoviruses (accuracy = 80.2%, binomial confidence interval [CI]: 70.8–87.6%), the sites informing predictions have no known involvement in virus binding and instead recapitulate host phylogeny.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of feature importance in the models, showing that selected sites are phylogenetically informative rather than mechanistically linked to binding.

claim: Models trained on host phylogeny alone performed equally well with an accuracy of 84.4% (CI: 75.5–91.0%).
source: Models trained on host phylogeny alone performed equally well (accuracy = 84.4%, CI: 75.5–91.0%) and at a level equivalent to retrospective assessments of accuracy for previously published models.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from machine learning models trained on phylogenetic eigenvectors.

claim: The predictive power of ACE2-based models derives from strong correlations with host phylogeny rather than processes which can be mechanistically linked to infection biology.
source: These results suggest that the predictive power of ACE2-based models derives from strong correlations with host phylogeny rather than processes which can be mechanistically linked to infection biology.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that phylogeny-only models perform as well as ACE2-based models and that ACE2 phylogeny closely matches host phylogeny.

claim: Biased availability of ACE2 sequences misleads projections of the number and geographic distribution of at-risk species.
source: Further, biased availability of ACE2 sequences misleads projections of the number and geographic distribution of at-risk species.
evidence: This is supported by data showing geographic biases in ACE2 sequence availability and their effect on predicted susceptibility hotspots.

claim: Models based on host phylogeny reduce bias from ACE2 sequence availability but identify a very large number of susceptible species.
source: Models based on host phylogeny reduce this bias, but identify a very large number of susceptible species, implying that model predictions must be combined with local knowledge of exposure risk to practically guide surveillance.
evidence: This is supported by data showing that phylogeny-based models predict 42.7% of mammals as susceptible (N=1785 species).

claim: Household transmission of SARS-CoV-2 to domestic dogs and cats has been reported.
source: For example, reports have described household transmission to domestic dogs and cats, transmission to lions and tigers in zoos, transmission to farmed mink, and transmission to free-living white-tailed deer (Barrs et al., 2020; Kuchipudi et al., 2022; McAloose et al., 2020; Sit et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published reports.

claim: Transmission of SARS-CoV-2 to lions and tigers in zoos has been reported.
source: For example, reports have described household transmission to domestic dogs and cats, transmission to lions and tigers in zoos, transmission to farmed mink, and transmission to free-living white-tailed deer (Barrs et al., 2020; Kuchipudi et al., 2022; McAloose et al., 2020; Sit et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published reports.

claim: Transmission of SARS-CoV-2 to farmed mink has been reported.
source: For example, reports have described household transmission to domestic dogs and cats, transmission to lions and tigers in zoos, transmission to farmed mink, and transmission to free-living white-tailed deer (Barrs et al., 2020; Kuchipudi et al., 2022; McAloose et al., 2020; Sit et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published reports.

claim: Transmission of SARS-CoV-2 to free-living white-tailed deer has been reported.
source: For example, reports have described household transmission to domestic dogs and cats, transmission to lions and tigers in zoos, transmission to farmed mink, and transmission to free-living white-tailed deer (Barrs et al., 2020; Kuchipudi et al., 2022; McAloose et al., 2020; Sit et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published reports.

claim: Repeated introductions of SARS-CoV-2 followed by onward transmission have been reported in both European mink and North American deer.
source: While the majority of such spillovers are likely to be dead-ends for the virus, repeated introductions followed by onward transmission have been reported in both European mink and North American deer (Kuchipudi et al., 2022; Oreshkova et al., 2020; Oude Munnink et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published reports.

claim: Animal infection experiments have demonstrated that a broad range of species spanning multiple mammalian orders are susceptible to SARS-CoV-2.
source: Animal infection experiments have demonstrated that a broad range of species spanning multiple mammalian orders are susceptible (Freuling et al., 2020; Munster et al., 2020; Mykytyn et al., 2021; Schlottau et al., 2020; Shi et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Egyptian fruit bats (Rousettus aegyptiacus) can be infected experimentally with SARS-CoV-2.
source: For example, Egyptian fruit bats (Rousettus aegyptiacus) can be infected experimentally with SARS-CoV-2, while attempts to establish infection in big brown bats (Eptesicus fuscus) have thus far failed (Hall et al., 2020; Schlottau et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Attempts to establish SARS-CoV-2 infection in big brown bats (Eptesicus fuscus) have thus far failed.
source: For example, Egyptian fruit bats (Rousettus aegyptiacus) can be infected experimentally with SARS-CoV-2, while attempts to establish infection in big brown bats (Eptesicus fuscus) have thus far failed (Hall et al., 2020; Schlottau et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Most computational heuristics for predicting SARS-CoV-2 host range utilise the amino acid sequence of ACE2 and base predictions on measures of similarity to human ACE2.
source: Most utilise the amino acid sequence of angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2, the host receptor involved in entry of SARS-CoV-2) and base predictions on measures of similarity to human ACE2, reasoning that changes relative to this sequence (particularly at amino acid positions known to interact with the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein) decrease the probability of successful infection (Ahmed et al., 2021; Alexander et al., 2020; Damas et al., 2020; Frank et al., 2020; Kumar et al., 2021; Luan et al., 2020; Melin et al., 2020; Qiu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple published heuristics.

claim: A structural approach has compared computational estimates of binding strength between modelled ACE2 protein structures of different species and the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein.
source: A related structural approach has compared computational estimates of binding strength (here grouped together as 'binding affinity') between the modelled ACE2 protein structures of different species and the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein, reasoning that stronger binding supports susceptibility (Huang et al., 2020; Lam et al., 2020; Rodrigues et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: An approach predicted whether binding strength was above a fixed threshold assumed to represent susceptibility and capacity for onward transmission, using ecological and physiological traits of host species.
source: A final approach predicted whether binding strength was above a fixed threshold which was assumed to represent susceptibility and capacity for onward transmission, using ecological and physiological traits of host species (Fischhoff et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: The final dataset contained records of interactions between sarbecoviruses and 96 mammalian and avian host species.
source: Our final dataset contained records of interactions between sarbecoviruses and 96 mammalian and avian host species.
evidence: This describes the dataset compiled for the study.

claim: The dataset included 25 species with natural infections.
source: Reports included natural infections (N=25) and the outcomes of experimental inoculations of captive animals (N=28), where in both cases subsequent detection of viral RNA in, or virus isolation from, nasal or rectal swabs or faeces was considered evidence of susceptibility.
evidence: This describes the composition of the dataset.

claim: The dataset included 28 species with experimental inoculations.
source: Reports included natural infections (N=25) and the outcomes of experimental inoculations of captive animals (N=28), where in both cases subsequent detection of viral RNA in, or virus isolation from, nasal or rectal swabs or faeces was considered evidence of susceptibility.
evidence: This describes the composition of the dataset.

claim: Data on whether species shed infectious virus were limited to 23 species, of which only 17 shed infectious virus.
source: We also separately recorded whether species were shown to shed infectious virus (either through virus isolation or infection of other animals), but available data were limited to 23 species, of which only 17 shed infectious virus (Figure 1).
evidence: This describes the limited availability of data on virus shedding.

claim: 88% of susceptible species in the dataset have been linked to at least one sarbecovirus known to use the ACE2 receptor.
source: In support of this assumption, most susceptible species in our data (88%) have been linked to at least one sarbecovirus known to use the ACE2 receptor, and among the 10 included host species with records of natural SARS-CoV-2 infection, many were also reported to be susceptible to other sarbecoviruses (N=6), primarily SARS-CoV (N=5, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of the compiled dataset.

claim: Among the 10 host species with records of natural SARS-CoV-2 infection, 6 were also reported to be susceptible to other sarbecoviruses.
source: In support of this assumption, most susceptible species in our data (88%) have been linked to at least one sarbecovirus known to use the ACE2 receptor, and among the 10 included host species with records of natural SARS-CoV-2 infection, many were also reported to be susceptible to other sarbecoviruses (N=6), primarily SARS-CoV (N=5, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of the compiled dataset.

claim: Sarbecovirus susceptibility was highly conserved within both host phylogenies (Pagel's λ>0.686, likelihood ratio test p-values ≤0.003).
source: Sarbecovirus susceptibility was highly conserved within both host phylogenies (Pagel's λ>0.686, likelihood ratio test p-values ≤0.003; Figure 1A–B).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of phylogenetic clustering.

claim: Non-susceptible species tended to be closer to other non-susceptible species than known susceptible host species, both in terms of divergence dates and ACE2 amino acid distances.
source: Clustering was particularly strong among non-susceptible species, which tended to be closer to other non-susceptible species than known susceptible host species, both in terms of divergence dates and ACE2 amino acid distances (Figure 1C–F).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of pairwise distances shown in Figure 1C-F.

claim: A phylogeny based on all available ACE2 ortholog sequences closely matched the topology and branch lengths of the time-scaled phylogeny (Baker's γ correlation coefficient = 0.934, permutation test p-value <0.001; Spearman's ρ correlation of pairwise distances = 0.870).
source: Further, a phylogeny based on all available ACE2 ortholog sequences closely matched the topology and branch lengths of the time-scaled phylogeny (Baker's γ correlation coefficient = 0.934, permutation test p-value <0.001; Spearman's ρ correlation of pairwise distances = 0.870, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of phylogenies.

claim: No ACE2 representation performed markedly better than a null model in terms of sensitivity.
source: In terms of sensitivity, no ACE2 representation performed markedly better than a null model which randomly assigned species as 'susceptible' or 'non-susceptible' in proportion to the frequency of susceptible species in the training data (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by model performance data shown in Figure 2.

claim: All ACE2 representations outperformed the null model in terms of specificity.
source: In contrast, specificity varied more dramatically among representations and all outperformed the null model, indicating that ACE2 can rule out non-susceptible species.
evidence: This is supported by model performance data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Only two models (using either the AA consensus distance or AA properties representations) clearly outperformed the null in terms of overall accuracy.
source: However, since non-susceptible species were rare in our training data (N=21), only two models (using either the AA consensus distance or AA properties representations) clearly outperformed the null in terms of overall accuracy.
evidence: This is supported by model performance data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The best-performing model (AA consensus distance) correctly predicted the susceptibility or non-susceptibility of 77 of 96 species (80.2%, 95% binomial confidence interval [CI]: 70.8–87.6%).
source: The best-performing model (AA consensus distance) correctly predicted the susceptibility or non-susceptibility of 77 of 96 species (80.2%, 95% binomial confidence interval [CI]: 70.8–87.6%).
evidence: This is supported by model performance data.

claim: Encoding ACE2 amino acid distances relative to the closest susceptible species ('distance to susceptible') outperformed the widely used metric of distance to human ACE2 ('distance to humans') in terms of specificity while maintaining high sensitivity.
source: Among other models, we found that encoding ACE2 amino acid distances relative to the closest susceptible species ('distance to susceptible') outperformed the widely used metric of distance to human ACE2 ('distance to humans') in terms of specificity while maintaining high sensitivity.
evidence: This is supported by model performance comparisons shown in Figure 2.

claim: The AA categorical model performed considerably worse than the null across all performance metrics.
source: The AA categorical model performed considerably worse than the null across all performance metrics (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by model performance data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Combining all representations of ACE2 had little effect on performance (74.0% accurate, CI: 64.0–82.4%).
source: Combining all representations of ACE2 had little effect on performance (74.0% accurate, CI: 64.0–82.4%), suggesting that divergence at key ACE2 amino acids from the susceptible consensus (and most other possible representations of ACE2 sequences) and structural models of binding affinity supply equivalent information.
evidence: This is supported by model performance data.

claim: The phylogeny-only model correctly predicted susceptibility labels of 81 species (84.4%, CI: 75.5–91.0%).
source: The phylogeny-only model performed equivalently to the best ACE2-only models, correctly predicting susceptibility labels of 81 species (84.4%, CI: 75.5–91.0%) with a nearly identical sensitivity alongside improved specificity ('phylogenetic eigenvectors', Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by model performance data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Combining phylogeny with either the best-performing ACE2 representation or all ACE2 representations performed similarly to phylogeny alone.
source: Combining phylogeny with either the best-performing ACE2 representation or all ACE2 representations performed similarly to phylogeny alone (Figure 2), suggesting that ACE2 sequences and measures of binding affinity supply information that is redundant with host divergence patterns.
evidence: This is supported by model performance data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The model trained with all ACE2-representations retained 25 features, of which just two were clearly linked to virus interaction.
source: The model trained with all ACE2-representations (but not phylogeny) retained 25 features, of which just two were clearly linked to virus interaction (both representations of binding affinity, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by feature importance analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Only one of the 18 ACE2 positions used by the model is known to interact with the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein (position 82).
source: Notably, only one of these positions is known to interact with the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein (position 82), but included positions did contain more phylogenetic information than average (as measured by Shannon entropy, Figure 3; Wilcoxon rank sum test p-value <0.001), suggesting they largely reconstructed host phylogeny.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of selected features shown in Figure 3.

claim: Included ACE2 positions contained more phylogenetic information than average (as measured by Shannon entropy, Wilcoxon rank sum test p-value <0.001).
source: Notably, only one of these positions is known to interact with the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein (position 82), but included positions did contain more phylogenetic information than average (as measured by Shannon entropy, Figure 3; Wilcoxon rank sum test p-value <0.001), suggesting they largely reconstructed host phylogeny.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: The best-performing ACE2-only model (AA consensus distance) retained no known spike-binding sites.
source: Similar results were observed in the best-performing ACE2-only model (the individual site-based 'AA consensus distance' model), which retained no known spike-binding sites (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by feature importance analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: A model based only on spike-binding sites performed considerably worse than other ACE2-based models.
source: However, it is unclear why the same sites would have been repeatedly selected from among the large number of correlated alternatives (Figure 3), and why they would be consistently preferred over spike-interacting sites themselves. Further, a model based only on spike-binding sites performed considerably worse than other ACE2-based models (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by model performance data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Strong correlations exist between predictions from the combined ACE2-based model and those from earlier studies.
source: Strong correlations between predictions from our combined ACE2-based model and those from earlier studies confirmed that it was broadly representative of earlier approaches (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Binding affinity-based predictions performed best among previously published heuristics.
source: However, performance appeared to be broadly similar across studies, with binding affinity-based predictions performing best (Huang et al., 2020), followed by distance-based and finally host trait-based approaches (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by retrospective performance assessment shown in Figure 4.

claim: Most distance-based approaches achieved their high accuracy by prioritising sensitivity and had very low specificity.
source: Most distance-based approaches achieved their high accuracy by prioritising sensitivity (i.e., accurate prediction of susceptible species, which dominate current data), and had very low specificity (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by performance analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The best ACE2-based model predicted 87.6% of mammals to be susceptible (N=178).
source: Our best-performing ACE2-based model, the AA consensus distance/AA consensus distance ensemble, predicted 87.6% of mammals to be susceptible (N=178).
evidence: This is supported by predictions from the trained model.

claim: 82.2% of mammals in available data are reported to be susceptible (N=90).
source: This is broadly in line with currently available data, where 82.2% of mammals are reported to be susceptible (N=90; Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by the compiled dataset shown in Figure 1.

claim: Species in South-East Asia were not more likely to be susceptible to sarbecoviruses than expected by chance.
source: However, species in this region were not more likely to be susceptible to sarbecoviruses than expected by chance (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by spatial analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The observed concentration of putatively susceptible species in South-East Asia appears to be shaped largely by the increased availability of ACE2 sequences for species from this region.
source: Instead, the observed concentration of putatively susceptible species appears to be shaped largely by the increased availability of ACE2 sequences for species from this region (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of ACE2 sequence availability and predicted susceptibility shown in Figure 5.

claim: The phylogeny-only model reduces the proportion of susceptible mammals from 87.6% to 42.7% (N=4183), implying the need for surveillance in 1785 mammal species.
source: By allowing predictions on species without available ACE2 sequences, the phylogeny-only model leads to different conclusions on how surveillance might be targeted. This model reduces the proportion of susceptible mammals from 87.6% to 42.7% (N=4183), but this still implies the need for surveillance in 1785 mammal species (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by predictions from the phylogeny-based model.

claim: In most mammalian taxonomic orders that contained susceptible species, all included species were predicted to be susceptible.
source: Consistent with observed data, in most mammalian taxonomic orders that contained susceptible species, all included species were predicted to be susceptible (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by taxonomic analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Primates, rodents, and bats contained several families with no species predicted as susceptible.
source: Interestingly however, primates, rodents, and bats deviated from this pattern, containing several families with no species predicted as susceptible (Figure 5—figure supplement 3, Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by taxonomic analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3 and 4.

claim: Susceptibility to sarbecovirus infection was highly conserved, clustering in patterns consistent with the evolutionary history of potential host species.
source: First, susceptibility to sarbecovirus infection was highly conserved, clustering in patterns consistent with the evolutionary history of potential host species.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis showing high Pagel's λ values.

claim: ACE2 is evolutionarily conserved, and a phylogeny derived from ACE2 sequences was highly congruent with one reflecting broader evolutionary history.
source: Second, ACE2 is also evolutionarily conserved, and a phylogeny derived from ACE2 sequences was highly congruent with one reflecting broader evolutionary history.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic comparison showing high correlation coefficients.

claim: Commonly used approaches for representing ACE2 sequence differences are largely equivalent in the amount of susceptibility information carried.
source: Third, commonly used approaches for representing ACE2 sequence differences are largely equivalent in the amount of susceptibility information carried (Figure 2, Figure 4—figure supplement 1), despite measuring biologically distinct aspects of ACE2 sequence variation and its interaction with sarbecovirus spike proteins.
evidence: This is supported by model performance comparisons and correlation analysis.

claim: Models based on host evolutionary history performed similarly to the best ACE2-based models.
source: Fourth, models based on host evolutionary history performed similarly to the best ACE2-based models, while considering ACE2 in addition to evolutionary history provided no detectable improvements.
evidence: This is supported by model performance comparisons shown in Figure 2.

claim: In ACE2-based models with access to information about individual amino acid positions, most predictive power was derived from phylogenetically-informative sites rather than virus-binding sites.
source: Finally, in ACE2-based models with access to information about individual amino acid positions, most predictive power was derived from phylogenetically-informative sites rather than virus-binding sites, even when measures of binding affinity and sequence similarity were removed.
evidence: This is supported by feature importance analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: The same features and sites were used across all species without affecting predictive accuracy for both rhinolophid bats and other species.
source: This held true for both rhinolophid bats (the putative ancestral hosts of sarbecoviruses which may have different host-virus interactions due to long-term co-evolutionary dynamics) and other species, with the same features and sites used across all species without affecting predictive accuracy (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by feature importance analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and 3.

claim: There is experimental evidence suggesting that variation in ACE2 alone can block infection.
source: While there is experimental evidence suggesting that variation in ACE2 alone can block infection (e.g., Guo et al., 2020; Thakur et al., 2022), how widely alleles conferring complete resistance occur in nature (particularly in species with no history of sarbecovirus exposure) remains unclear.
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: A broad diversity of ACE2 variation is permissive for infection.
source: Indeed, our data show that a broad diversity of ACE2 variation is permissive for infection, so such examples, though biologically verified, may be extremes that do not generalise across taxa.
evidence: This is inferred from the high proportion of susceptible species across diverse ACE2 sequences in the dataset.

claim: Sarbecovirus host range is likely to be shaped by a range of factors all showing some level of phylogenetic conservation.
source: Instead, sarbecovirus host range is likely to be shaped by a range of factors all showing some level of phylogenetic conservation (e.g., receptor distribution, innate immunity, behaviour).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that phylogeny alone predicts susceptibility as well as ACE2.

claim: ACE2 sequences are only available for a small fraction of potential host species.
source: A key drawback of ACE2-based models is that data are only available for a small fraction of potential host species (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by the geographic distribution of ACE2 sequence availability shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Many ACE2 sequences likely stem from existing sarbecovirus research which is geographically biased.
source: This limits their applied use and may also introduce biases since many ACE2 sequences likely stem from existing sarbecovirus research which is geographically biased.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed geographic concentration of ACE2 sequences.

claim: The host trait-based approach appeared to have reduced performance relative to models directly incorporating host phylogeny.
source: However, although we reiterate that quantitative measures of performance should be considered cautiously, this approach appeared to have reduced performance relative to models directly incorporating host phylogeny (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by performance comparisons shown in Figure 4.

claim: 11 of 12 species more recently reported as naturally infected were accurately predicted by the phylogeny-based model.
source: Anecdotally, this accuracy extends to species only recognised as susceptible after data collection for this study had ended, with 11 of 12 species more recently reported as naturally infected accurately predicted by the phylogeny-based model (Supplementary file 2; Allender et al., 2022; Kuchipudi et al., 2022; Padilla-Blanco et al., 2022; Pereira et al., 2022; United States Department of Agriculture, 2022; United States Department of Agriculture, 2021a; United States Department of Agriculture, 2021b; United States Department of Agriculture, 2021c; Wang et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by post-hoc validation using newly reported infections.

claim: 65.2% of mammals tested in experimental infections were susceptible (CI: 42.7–83.6%).
source: This issue does not stem from the models, which show high accuracy on current data, but rather are representative of a pattern of widespread susceptibility seen consistently across experimental infections (65.2% of mammals susceptible, CI: 42.7–83.6%), our wider training data (82.2%, CI: 72.7–89.5%), and predictions from both the ACE2-based ensemble and host phylogeny-based models (87.6% and 42.6%, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of experimental infection data.

claim: Conditioning predictions on the top 30% of species captures the majority of currently known susceptibles (73%), but still means at least 1255 mammals require surveillance.
source: However, while conditioning our predictions on the top 30% of species captures the majority of currently known susceptibles (73%), this still means at least 1255 mammals require surveillance while introducing a significant risk of missing key spillovers (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of prediction thresholds shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The majority of susceptible hosts are unlikely to transmit the virus effectively.
source: Looking further into the future, our data suggest that the majority of susceptible hosts are unlikely to transmit the virus effectively (Figure 1A), and indeed only a limited number of natural spillovers have thus far resulted in onward transmission (Kuchipudi et al., 2022; Oude Munnink et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by data on virus shedding shown in Figure 1A and citations to transmission studies.

claim: Current data cannot produce models capable of accurately predicting virus shedding.
source: However, the inability of current data to produce models capable of accurately predicting virus shedding (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) indicates a need for greater investment to gather sufficient data on the ability of hosts to transmit sarbecoviruses.
evidence: This is supported by model performance data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The relatively small number of species for which sarbecovirus susceptibility data are available is a clear limitation of the approach.
source: A clear limitation of our approach is the relatively small number of species for which sarbecovirus susceptibility data are available.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the limitations of the study.

claim: Limited numbers of known non-susceptible species made it difficult to distinguish variation in the specificity of alternative approaches with confidence.
source: Combining diverse data sources and expanding the scope to all sarbecoviruses allowed us to evaluate the rapidly growing number of untested heuristics predicting SARS-CoV-2 host range. However, limited numbers of known non-susceptible species in particular made it difficult to distinguish variation in the specificity of alternative approaches with confidence, a problem exacerbated by low levels of overlap between available data and the species for which predictions were available in individual studies (wide CIs, Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the analysis, supported by wide confidence intervals in Figure 4B.

claim: There was no evidence to suggest that including data from cell culture-based experiments skewed results.
source: Although our strategy to maximise sample size meant including data from cell culture-based experiments, we found no evidence to suggest that this skewed results (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The inclusion of additional sarbecoviruses did not adversely impact model performance.
source: While previous approaches were not explicitly designed for non-SARS-CoV-2 sarbecoviruses, our results suggest the inclusion of additional sarbecoviruses did not adversely impact model performance (Figure 2—figure supplement 3, Figure 2—figure supplement 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by model performance analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3, 4, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Most species (90.8%) included in the dataset have been either linked to or tested for susceptibility to sarbecoviruses known to use ACE2 as an entry receptor.
source: This may be because most species (90.8%) included in our dataset have been either linked to or tested for susceptibility to sarbecoviruses known to use ACE2 as an entry receptor (Khaledian et al., 2022; Starr et al., 2022), including all non-susceptible species (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of the dataset composition.

claim: Nine susceptible host species have so far only been reported to be infected by sarbecoviruses which are either not known to use ACE2 or are suspected to use an alternative receptor.
source: Nine susceptible host species have so far only been reported to be infected by sarbecoviruses which are either not known to use ACE2 (due to a lack of published experiments involving the viruses in question) or are suspected to use an alternative receptor (based on an inability to bind the ACE2 orthologs tested thus far); we detected no differences in accuracy when predicting the susceptibility of these species (Figure 2—figure supplement 3, Figure 2—figure supplement 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of model performance on different subsets of species.

claim: No differences in accuracy were detected when predicting the susceptibility of species linked only to non-ACE2-utilising sarbecoviruses.
source: Nine susceptible host species have so far only been reported to be infected by sarbecoviruses which are either not known to use ACE2 (due to a lack of published experiments involving the viruses in question) or are suspected to use an alternative receptor (based on an inability to bind the ACE2 orthologs tested thus far); we detected no differences in accuracy when predicting the susceptibility of these species (Figure 2—figure supplement 3, Figure 2—figure supplement 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by model performance analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3, 4, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Convergence in performance for viruses that putatively use different receptors lends further support to the conclusion that sarbecovirus host range is determined by factors other than ACE2 sequence variation.
source: This convergence in performance for viruses that putatively use different receptors lends further support to our conclusion that sarbecovirus host range is determined by factors other than ACE2 sequence variation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that models perform similarly for species linked to different sarbecoviruses.

claim: Available susceptibility data may be affected by the same taxonomic and geographic biases affecting ACE2 sequence availability.
source: Finally, available susceptibility data may be affected by the same taxonomic and geographic biases affecting ACE2 sequence availability.
evidence: This is speculation about potential biases in the data.

claim: Directly observed data will be biased to countries with capacity for surveillance.
source: For example, directly observed data will be biased to countries with capacity for surveillance, in vivo data will be limited to animal models that can be maintained in captivity, and heterologous ACE2 experiments are limited by requiring prior knowledge of ACE2 sequences.
evidence: This is speculation about potential sources of bias in the data.

claim: In vivo data will be limited to animal models that can be maintained in captivity.
source: For example, directly observed data will be biased to countries with capacity for surveillance, in vivo data will be limited to animal models that can be maintained in captivity, and heterologous ACE2 experiments are limited by requiring prior knowledge of ACE2 sequences.
evidence: This is speculation about potential sources of bias in the data.

claim: Current biases could not produce a false equivalence between ACE2 sequences and host phylogeny.
source: However, while this implies that predictions could be periodically updated as new observations become available, we see no mechanism through which current biases could produce a false equivalence between ACE2 sequences and host phylogeny.
evidence: This is an inference about the robustness of the main finding.

claim: Both current data and model predictions suggest a significant ongoing risk of reverse zoonosis to a wide range of species.
source: Our results imply major challenges for predicting the host range of generalist viruses such as SARS-CoV-2, even when models are reasonably accurate. Both current data and model predictions suggest a significant ongoing risk of reverse zoonosis to a wide range of species, implying a need for continued surveillance among species in contact with humans.
evidence: This is an inference based on the high proportion of susceptible species predicted by models.
